name: Quechua II
region: From southern Colombia and Ecuador through northern and southern Peru to Bolivia and northwest Argentina
defining_innovation: The peripheral branch that spread north and south from central Peru. One of its southern varieties became the common language of the Inca empire and then the missionary 'general language'.

chapters.title: An Imperial Language
chapters.body:
Quechua II surrounds Central Quechua on both sides. Torero divided it into II-A in the northern Peruvian highlands, II-B in Ecuador, Colombia and the Peruvian Amazon, and II-C in southern Peru, Bolivia and Argentina. Its spread was partly the work of trade along the coast before the Inca, and partly of the Inca themselves, who used a southern variety across their empire in the 15th century. After the conquest, the Spanish kept that role going: missionaries preached, wrote and printed in a standardised *lengua general*.

The first grammar of the language, published in 1560 by the Dominican **Domingo de Santo Tomás**, describes a coastal Quechua II variety.

chapters.title: The Written Colonial Language
chapters.body:
Quechua II is the branch in which almost all early Quechua writing was done. The Jesuit Diego González Holguín published a grammar of the Cusco language in 1607 and a large Quechua–Spanish dictionary in 1608. His *Vocabulario* records thousands of words and idioms and is still consulted for the meaning of older terms.

The same years produced the most remarkable Quechua text of the colonial period, the Huarochirí Manuscript of about 1608. It is an anonymous collection of myths and religious practices from the highlands east of Lima, gathered in connection with the campaign against 'idolatry' led by the priest Francisco de Ávila. Although collected in a Central Quechua region, it is written in a form close to the colonial general language. It is the only extensive account of Andean religion written in an Andean language.

The Andean chronicler Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala included Quechua songs and speeches in his illustrated letter to the Spanish king of about 1615. In the 18th century the Quechua drama *Ollantay*, set in the Inca court, became the best-known work of the language's literature. Its date and author are uncertain, and scholars still debate how much it owes to Spanish Golden Age theatre.

speakers.note: Nearly all of the total is Southern Quechua in Peru and Bolivia; northern varieties are far smaller and more endangered.

turning_points.title: The language of Tawantinsuyu
turning_points.description: The expanding Inca state uses a Quechua II variety as its language of administration across the empire, carrying it to Ecuador, Bolivia and Argentina. What the Inca court spoke originally, perhaps Aymara or Puquina, is disputed.

sources.citation: Adelaar, Willem F. H. with Pieter C. Muysken. 2004. The Languages of the Andes. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
Cerrón-Palomino, Rodolfo. 2013. Las lenguas de los incas: el puquina, el aimara y el quechua. Frankfurt am Main: Peter Lang.

turning_points.title: The first Quechua grammar
turning_points.description: Domingo de Santo Tomás publishes in Valladolid the *Grammatica o arte de la lengua general de los indios de los reynos del Peru* and a dictionary, writing Quechua in the Latin alphabet for missionary use.

sources.citation: Santo Tomás, Domingo de. 1560. Grammatica o arte de la lengua general de los indios de los reynos del Peru. Valladolid: Francisco Fernández de Córdova.
Adelaar, Willem F. H. with Pieter C. Muysken. 2004. The Languages of the Andes. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

contested_classifications.proposed_grouping: Torero's II-A / II-B / II-C: three clean subgroups of Quechua II
contested_classifications.evidence_for: The division fits the main isoglosses and is the standard reference classification, used in most descriptions and in Glottolog's broad outline.
contested_classifications.evidence_against: Quechua forms a dialect continuum, and transitional varieties such as Pacaraos and those of Yauyos do not fit neatly. II-A in particular may be a geographical collection rather than a true subgroup, and the close ties of II-B and II-C may reflect the Inca and colonial spread rather than descent.

sources.citation: Adelaar, Willem F. H. with Pieter C. Muysken. 2004. The Languages of the Andes. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
